energy-state-comparison-map.title: Energy conservation compares system states without solving motion

claims.title: Compare states
claims.statement: Energy accounting can relate two mechanical states without reconstructing what happened between them.

claims.title: Use electrostatic energy
claims.statement: The passage introduces energy conservation as a useful way to investigate electrostatic systems.

claims.title: No trajectory supplied
claims.statement: Comparing states through energy does not itself specify the intervening motion.

claims.title: Repulsion releases stored energy
claims.statement: Short-range ionic repulsion stores deformation energy that is released on separation, reducing dissociation work.

claims.title: Compressibility estimate
claims.statement: The source reports a compressibility-based repulsive contribution of about one ninth-point-four of the attractive contribution, with the opposite sign.

claims.title: Prediction and measured work
claims.statement: Subtracting the repulsive contribution gives the source-reported 7.99 eV per NaCl formula unit, closer to its observed 7.92 eV.

claims.title: Vibration amount unspecified
claims.statement: The source also invokes crystal-vibration kinetic energy but supplies no numerical vibration correction or microscopic dynamical model.

claims.title: Electrostatic contribution dominates
claims.statement: The passage interprets the corrected comparison as support for electrostatics being the main contribution to NaCl crystal binding.

nuclear-dependencies-map.title: Nuclear force depends on distance, spin and motion

claims.title: Several interaction dependencies
claims.statement: The source rejects a universal scalar separation law for the described nucleon interaction.

claims.title: Distance dependence
claims.statement: The source describes attraction at larger separations and repulsion at closer separations, without specifying a numerical potential.

claims.title: Relative spin directions
claims.statement: Changing the relative spin directions changes the described interaction.

claims.title: Separation direction versus spins
claims.statement: The direction of separation relative to the spin axes also changes the described interaction.

claims.title: Motion and spin–orbit alignment
claims.statement: Relative motion and the sense of orbital rotation compared with spin are additional dependencies.

claims.title: Historical mechanism statement
claims.statement: The source’s claims about incomplete knowledge describe its historical account; the passage supplies no quantitative nuclear force or scattering law.

nuclear-component-symmetry-map.title: Approximate charge independence of nuclear interactions

claims.title: Nuclear-component symmetry
claims.statement: In the source’s charge-independence approximation, substituting proton and neutron leaves the nuclear component of their interactions unchanged.

claims.title: Electrical contribution is separate
claims.statement: This comparison concerns the nuclear component; it is not equality of the complete forces including electrical effects.

claims.title: Broader strong-interaction symmetry
claims.statement: The passage connects this substitution principle to a broader symmetry of strongly interacting particles.

claims.title: Historical explanation statement
claims.statement: The statement that the fundamental reason is unknown belongs to the source’s historical discussion.

claims.title: Tentative core and outer particle
claims.statement: The passage tentatively describes the extra particle as outside a core containing five protons and five neutrons.

claims.title: Five-versus-six Coulomb cost
claims.statement: Under that geometry, adding an outside proton costs ZB qe²/(4π ε0 r), five sixths of the preceding uniform-model energy difference.

claims.title: Conditional radius comparison
claims.statement: For the same inferred energy difference, the radius is five sixths of the preceding estimate and is reported to agree more closely with direct measurements.

claims.title: Source-era conclusions
claims.statement: The passage interprets the agreement as support for electrical laws at nuclear distances and equality of the nonelectrical nucleon interactions; these are its historical inferences.
